provenance.other: “because of unbelief” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Romans 11:20, Hebrews 3:19 and Hebrews 4:6. The two Hebrews verses are about the wilderness generation failing to enter the rest; only Romans 11:20 makes unbelief the cause of a branch being broken off from Israel, which is the figure Jacob has been running since 10:1.
provenance.significance: Jacob opens the chapter 'concerning this righteous branch', and the first thing he says about it is that children will perish 'because of unbelief' and then 'be restored'. That is the shape of Romans 11 in two clauses: broken off because of unbelief (11:20), graffed in again if they abide not still in unbelief (11:23). Recover the context and the metalepsis is sharp — Paul's warning is addressed to the Gentile branch not to boast over the natural one, and Jacob's chapter goes on to promise the land to Gentiles who are 'numbered among the house of Israel' (10:18). The suppressed premise of Romans 11 is exactly the premise of Jacob's sermon.

10:2.note: 'Many of our children shall perish in the flesh, because of unbelief... and our children shall be restored.' The verbal contact is three words, but they are the three words of Romans 11:20 and they arrive attached to the branch of 10:1 and the breaking-off of 10:22 — the two other load-bearing terms of the same Pauline paragraph. Below any quotation threshold, Skousen's included; the case rests on the co-occurrence, not the length.
10:2.text: Well; because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear:

provenance.alternative: The bare 'they shall crucify him' is Jacob's own, adjudicated at 2 Nephi 6:9 against Matthew 20:19; nothing here requires a second source.
provenance.significance: 'There is none other nation on earth that would crucify their God' is a claim about counterfactual national responses to a divine visitor, and the KJV has one verse that makes such a claim: 'had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.' Paul excuses the crucifiers by ignorance; Jacob incriminates them by election, arguing that Jerusalem alone was wicked enough to do it. The two verses answer the same question in opposite directions, which is why the echo is worth recording even though the shared vocabulary is one word.

10:3.note: Written under CONVENTIONS 0a as a link worth putting on the table. The argument is structural, not verbal: 1 Corinthians 2:8 is the only KJV verse that asks what a nation would have done had it known whom it was crucifying, and 2 Nephi 10:3-4 is a sustained answer to that question, continued in 10:4's counterfactual about the other nations.
10:3.whyNot: One shared word, 'crucify', and it is the unavoidable word for the event. A reader who declines this link loses nothing from the chapter; the surrounding argument runs on Matthew 11:21 (10:4), which has real verbal contact.
10:3.text: Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

provenance.other: “they would have repented” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:21. Luke's parallel at 10:13 recasts it as 'they had a great while ago repented', so the Book of Mormon's counterfactual has Matthew's form of the verb, not Luke's. 'Mighty works' (10 KJV verses) becomes 'mighty miracles', which is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:21-23 is the KJV's one sustained argument that a city which saw the miracles is guiltier than the pagan cities that did not: Tyre and Sidon would have repented, Sodom would have remained. 2 Nephi 10:4-5 reproduces that argument entire and then names its target — 'they at Jerusalem will stiffen their necks against him' — putting Jerusalem in Capernaum's place. Recover Matthew's context and the substitution is the point: the oracle Jesus pronounced against the towns of Galilee is here pronounced against the city that crucified him.

10:4.note: 'For should the mighty miracles be wrought among other nations, they would repent, and know that he be their God; but because of priest-crafts and iniquities, they at Jerusalem will stiffen their necks.' The counterfactual, the comparison class of other nations, and the verdict against the city that actually saw the works are all Matthew 11:21-23, and the singleton 'they would have repented' anchors the wording. The machine stream proposed nothing at all for this verse, which is CONVENTIONS 9 in miniature: no contiguous window survives the substitution of 'mighty miracles' for 'mighty works'.
10:4.text: Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.

provenance.route: Luke 21:11, 21:24 / Matthew 24:7 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon (via Jacob's own list at 2 Nephi 6:15)
provenance.other: “famines, and pestilences” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:7 and Luke 21:11, in that order in both. mediation-check.py reports one 'decisive' point for Matthew, but it is an absence — the Book of Mormon lacks Luke's 'in divers places' — and an absence cannot decide between two verses that agree on everything the Book of Mormon reproduces. The mediation is left uncertain on the evidence of this verse.
provenance.significance: Jacob has already given this list once, at 2 Nephi 6:15, in the reverse order and with 'bloodsheds' added to the synoptic set. Here it returns compressed and forward-ordered. The interesting half of the verse is the second: 'they which shall not be destroyed shall be scattered among all nations' is the fate Luke 21:24 assigns to Jerusalem after the same catalogue of signs, and Jacob applies it to the same city.

10:6.note: A repeat of Jacob's own formula rather than a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING 4): the link is written because the discourse is continuous and the second half of the verse adds Luke 21:24, but the argument for the synoptic catalogue itself was made at 2 Nephi 6:15 and is not restated here.
10:6.text: And great earthquakes shall be in divers places, and famines, and pestilences; and fearful sights and great signs shall there be from heaven.

provenance.other: “islands of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11, and “four corners of the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 11:12 and Revelation 7:1. The Book of Mormon has 'isles of the sea' and 'four parts of the earth' — neither is the KJV's word, and both departures are consistent (see 10:21, where 'isles' is made to carry an argument).
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:11-12 is the KJV's one place where a gathering of the dispersed from the islands of the sea and from the four corners of the earth stand in adjacent verses, and 2 Nephi 10:8 fuses them into a single clause. Jacob has already invoked the first of the two at 6:14 ('set himself again the second time'), and his own book transcribes the whole chapter at 2 Nephi 21.

10:8.note: 'Gathered in from their long dispersion, from the isles of the sea, and from the four parts of the earth.' Two rare Isaiah 11 phrases in one sentence, each altered in the same direction — toward a commoner English word. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 at 10:21 rather than here; the fuller verbal contact is at 10:8 and the link is placed accordingly (CONVENTIONS 6a).
10:8.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

provenance.other: “nursing fathers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “nursing mothers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Isaiah 49:23; the singular “nursing father” is Numbers 11:12. Jacob transcribed the verse at 2 Nephi 6:7 and here returns to it as his own text.
provenance.significance: The clause is re-quoted with one substitution that carries the chapter: Isaiah's 'kings shall be THY nursing fathers' becomes 'the kings of the GENTILES shall be nursing fathers unto them'. Isaiah's second person is the daughter of Zion; Jacob has resolved the pronoun into a specific reading of who the kings are, and the rest of the chapter (10:10-11, 10:18-19) is built on that resolution.

10:9.note: A re-quotation inside an exposition, not a fresh borrowing: the transcription is at 2 Nephi 6:7 and the argument for it was made there. What is new here is the gloss — the identification of Isaiah's kings and queens as Gentiles, which the Isaiah verse does not make and which the whole land-promise of 10:10-19 depends on. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 49:22-23 at this verse.
10:9.text: And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 8:7 and 12:12 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: 'There shall be no kings upon the land' is a promise, and 10:14 gives the reason: 'he that raiseth up a king against me shall perish. For I the Lord, the King of Heaven, will be their king.' That is the theology of 1 Samuel 8 exactly — a human king is a rejection of the divine one, 'they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them' — and 1 Samuel 12:12 states the antithesis in the same terms Jacob does, 'a king shall reign over us: when the LORD your God was your king.' Nephi refused the crown at 2 Nephi 5:18 on Gideon's grounds; Jacob now makes the refusal a standing condition of the land.

10:11.note: No verbal borrowing to speak of — 'king' and 'reign' are the only shared words — so this is filed as a conceptual allusion, on the strength of a whole argument reproduced rather than a phrase. It matters because it is the scriptural warrant behind the chapter's most-quoted sentence, 'this land shall be a land of liberty', a phrase that is in no KJV verse at all.
10:11.whyNot: A reader may reasonably say that a monarchy-refusing land promise needs no source, and that 1 Samuel 8 is where any such argument in English would land by gravity rather than by borrowing.
10:11.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

provenance.other: “against mount Zion” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:8. The preceding verse, Isaiah 29:7, has 'fight against Ariel' where the Book of Mormon's own expansion of the chapter at 2 Nephi 27:3 reads 'fight against Zion' — so the Book of Mormon replaces Ariel with Zion at exactly the point where Jacob's formula needs it.
provenance.significance: Jacob's refrain 'he that fighteth against Zion shall perish' agrees with the Book of Mormon's Isaiah rather than with the KJV's. Isaiah 29:7-8 fights against Ariel and then against mount Zion; 2 Nephi 27:3 fights against Zion in both places; Jacob has the second form. The finding is internal: the phrase he treats as scriptural is the reading his own book will give of Isaiah 29 fifteen chapters later, not the reading a KJV reader would find at Isaiah 29:7.

10:13.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:8 here and the singleton 'against mount Zion' justifies it. The reason to keep the link at 10:13 rather than move it forward to the transcription is that Jacob is using the phrase as a fixed formula — he repeats it verbatim at 10:16 — which is what makes its agreement with 2 Nephi 27:3 worth recording. Flagged for Wilson: this is a within-book agreement pointing FORWARD to a chapter not yet adjudicated in this run, so the mediation is recorded as direct-OT rather than OT-via-earlier-BoM, which would be false about the order of the book.
10:13.text: It shall even be as when an hungry man dreameth, and, behold, he eateth; but he awaketh, and his soul is empty: or as when a thirsty man dreameth, and, behold, he drinketh; but he awaketh, and, behold, he is faint, and his soul hath appetite: so shall the multitude of all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion.

provenance.other: “the King of heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 4:37. “be a light unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 7:8 ('when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me'); the everlasting-light promise itself is Isaiah 60:19-20.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest piece of metalepsis. The KJV uses the title 'the King of heaven' once, and it is Nebuchadnezzar's confession after seven years of madness, ending 'and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.' Jacob's sentence is about kings: no king shall be raised up in this land, he that raiseth up a king shall perish, and the Lord will be their king instead. The one KJV verse that names God 'the King of heaven' is the verse in which the greatest king in scripture is abased for pride and made to say so. Neither text says this; the borrowed title says it.

10:14.note: 'For I the Lord, the King of Heaven, will be their king.' A three-word title, but an absolute singleton, and it lands in the one sentence of the chapter where a human king is being disposed of. The second half of the verse, 'I will be a light unto them forever', pairs a second singleton (Micah 7:8) with the everlasting light of Isaiah 60:19-20; the composite is recorded rather than split into separate rows because the sentence is one movement.
10:14.text: Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.

provenance.other: “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 and Ephesians 5:11. Romans 13:12 was the source adjudicated at 2 Nephi 1:23 ('put on the armour'), and it has nothing about secrecy; Ephesians 5:12 supplies it in the next breath — 'those things which are done of them in secret.' The Book of Mormon's 'secret works of darkness' fuses the two adjacent Ephesians verses, and the choice between the two 'works of darkness' verses is decided by the adjective.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:11-12 also supplies the company the phrase keeps here. Jacob's triad is 'the secret works of darkness, and of murders, and of abominations'; Ephesians 5:3-5 lists fornication, uncleanness and covetousness as the things not to be named, and 5:12 makes their secrecy the shameful part. What Jacob adds is murder, which turns a moral catalogue into a description of conspiracy — the reading the rest of the Book of Mormon will build on.

10:15.note: The discriminating evidence is the word 'secret'. Of the KJV's two 'works of darkness' verses only Ephesians has secrecy attached, and it is attached in the immediately following verse. Below any quotation threshold; the case is a two-verse fusion, not a reproduced clause.
10:15.text: And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.

provenance.route: Galatians 3:28, with 1 Corinthians 12:13's wording in the first pair -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “male nor female” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 3:28, and “bond nor free” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11. Only Galatians has all three pairs, and the Book of Mormon has them in Galatians' order. But Galatians reads 'neither Jew nor Greek', and the Book of Mormon reads 'both Jew and Gentile' — which is 1 Corinthians 12:13's pairing, 'whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free'. mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for this verse, because the two candidates do not differ at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces word for word; the discrimination has to be made from the singleton and the substituted pair instead.
provenance.significance: Paul's triad abolishes the distinctions inside Christ; Jacob's triad abolishes them inside a threat. 'Both Jew and Gentile, both bond and free, both male and female, shall perish' takes the KJV's one formula for the irrelevance of human categories and applies it to the categories of the damned. Recover Galatians 3:28's context — 'for ye are all one in Christ Jesus' — and the borrowing reads as a deliberate inversion: the same universality, opposite sign.

10:16.note: Three pairs, in one KJV verse's order, with one pair reworded toward a second KJV verse's vocabulary. The strength is the singleton 'male nor female'; the interest is that 'Jew and Gentile' is not Galatians' phrase and is 1 Corinthians'. The machine stream proposed Numbers 5:3 here on 'both male and female', which is excluded.
10:16.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.

provenance.route: Matthew 12:30 / Luke 11:23, with Luke 9:50's preposition -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “is not with me is against me” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 12:30 and Luke 11:23, and both read 'with me'. The Book of Mormon reads 'they which are not FOR me, are against me'. The KJV has one verse with the polarity stated that way round — Luke 9:50, 'he that is not against us is for us' — and it is the saying's mirror image, not this one.
provenance.significance: The two logia are famously opposite: Matthew 12:30 and Luke 11:23 exclude the neutral, Mark 9:40 and Luke 9:50 include them. The Book of Mormon has the exclusive saying's polarity with the inclusive saying's preposition, which is the sort of cross-contamination that happens when a formula is remembered rather than copied. It is worth recording precisely because it cannot be got from any single KJV verse.

10:16.note: 'They which are not for me, are against me, saith our God.' A short clause, but it is a KJV rarity and the one-word departure from it is the finding: 'for' where both source verses have 'with'. Flagged as the kind of case ADJUDICATING 4 warns about in reverse — here the window does not close early, it closes on a substituted preposition that only the other member of the pair uses.
10:16.text: He that is not with me is against me; and he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad.

provenance.other: “whore” occurs in exactly 65 KJV verses, almost all of them prophetic-adultery language in the Hebrew Bible. The great whore who is a corporate entity spanning the earth, rather than a figure for apostate Israel, is Revelation's: 17:5's 'MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH' and 19:2's 'the great whore, which did corrupt the earth'.
provenance.significance: 'The whore of all the earth' is a Book of Mormon coinage, but its two components are Revelation 17:5's genitive of scope and 19:2's earth-corrupting subject. What the borrowing does is make the whore a category rather than a city: Jacob's whore is not Babylon but everyone, of either nation and either sex, who fights against Zion.

10:16.note: Recorded at moderate because no clause is reproduced; the case is that the specific idea of a whore whose scope is the whole earth exists in the KJV only in Revelation 17-19. Below any quotation threshold and offered under CONVENTIONS 0a.
10:16.whyNot: 'Whore' is one of the commonest prophetic insults in the KJV and 'all the earth' is not rare; a reader who thinks Jacob has fused two ordinary biblical words without reference to Revelation is not obviously wrong.
10:16.text: And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.

provenance.other: “dwell upon the earth shall worship” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 13:8. The Book of Mormon has 'I will have all men that dwell thereon, that they shall worship me'.
provenance.significance: If the echo is real it is an inversion: the KJV's one sentence about all the earth's inhabitants worshipping is about the beast, and the names not written in the book of life. Jacob's land is consecrated on the same condition with the opposite object.

10:19.note: Proposed under CONVENTIONS 0a as a rarity worth putting on the table, and no more than that. The shared string is a singleton, but it is a singleton made of five of the commonest words in the KJV, which is exactly the profile of a coincidence.
10:19.whyNot: 'Dwell' and 'worship' are unavoidable words for the thought, and the Book of Mormon breaks the phrase across a relative clause ('that dwell thereon, that they shall worship me') rather than reproducing it. Nothing else in 10:19 has any contact with Revelation 13.
10:19.text: And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

provenance.route: Psalm 77:19 and Isaiah 43:16 -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “path in the” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and they are the same verse twice over: Psalm 77:19, 'Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters', and Isaiah 43:16, 'which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters'. Both pair 'way' with 'path' and both are about the Red Sea.
provenance.significance: 'The Lord hath made the sea our path' is the family's ocean crossing described in the only two KJV verses that put a path in the sea, and both of them mean the Exodus. The metalepsis is the Book of Mormon's standing one: recover the context of Psalm 77 and it is a psalm about remembering the years of the right hand of the most High, which ends 'Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.' Jacob's sentence — driven out of the land of our inheritance, led to a better land, the sea made our path — is the Exodus reused as the charter of a colony.

10:20.note: Two words of contact, but they are 'path' and 'sea' in the KJV's only two verses that join them, and the sentence they sit in is doing the Exodus typology the whole book runs on. The preceding clause, 'we are not cast off', is the language of Psalm 94:14 and Romans 11:1-2 and belongs with the Romans 11 argument at 10:2 rather than with this link.
10:20.text: Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known.

provenance.route: Isaiah 24:15 (and Isaiah 49:1) -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “isles of the sea” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Esther 10:1, where it is the extent of Ahasuerus's tribute, and Isaiah 24:15, where it is where the LORD's name is to be glorified. Isaiah 11:11 — the verse Hardy cross-references here, and the verse Jacob is expounding — reads 'islands of the sea', and so does the Book of Mormon's own transcription of it at 2 Nephi 21:11.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most interesting textual fact and it is an internal one. Jacob makes an exegetical argument out of a plural: 'as it sayeth ISLES, there must needs be more than this.' But the passage he is expounding does not say isles. It says islands — in the KJV at Isaiah 11:11, and in the Book of Mormon's own Isaiah at 2 Nephi 21:11. The word he exegetes is the word of Isaiah 24:15 and Isaiah 49:1 ('Listen, O isles, unto me'), the latter being the chapter Jacob had transcribed four chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 6.

10:21.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 at this verse, which is right about what Jacob is expounding and wrong about where the wording comes from; the fuller Isaiah 11:11 link is therefore placed at 10:8 and this row records the 'isles' crux (CONVENTIONS 6a). Flagged for Wilson: the observation that a Book of Mormon exegesis turns on a word its own transcription of the source does not contain is a finding about the book, not just about this verse, and may deserve a place in the front matter rather than a chapter row.
10:21.text: Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.

provenance.other: “broken off” occurs in exactly five KJV verses: Job 17:11 (purposes), Isaiah 27:11 (withered boughs), and Romans 11:17, 11:19 and 11:20, all of the olive-tree allegory. Three of the five are one paragraph of Romans, and it is the only KJV place where what is broken off is a part of Israel.
provenance.significance: The chapter closes its argument where it opened it. 10:1 announced 'this righteous branch'; 10:2 gave the reason for breaking off, 'because of unbelief'; 10:22 gives the remedy, 'the Lord remembereth all they which have been broken off.' Paul's point in Romans 11 is that the breaking-off is not final, and Jacob's application is that it is not even local — the branches broken off from the house of Israel 'from time to time' include his own family, 'wherefore, he remembereth us also.'

10:22.note: Adjudicated as a link rather than a bare recurrence because the phrase does work here that it did not do at 10:2 or at 2 Nephi 3:5: this is where the Romans 11 figure is applied to the Lehites themselves. The argument for the source was made at 10:2 and is not restated.
10:22.text: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;

provenance.route: Jeremiah 21:8, with Deuteronomy 30:19's framing -> KJV -> Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the way of life, and the way of death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 21:8. Deuteronomy 30:19 sets life and death before the people but does not call them ways; the Book of Mormon has Jeremiah's noun and Deuteronomy's imperative to choose.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 21:8 is spoken to a Jerusalem under siege, and the way of life it offers is surrender to Babylon — a way of life that looks like defeat. Jacob's audience is a colony that has been 'driven out of the land of our inheritance' (10:20), and he offers them the same choice in the same words, having just told them the exile was not abandonment. The metalepsis fits the chapter: the KJV verse that phrases the choice this way is addressed to people about to lose their land.

10:23.note: Hardy cross-references both Deuteronomy 30:19 and Jeremiah 21:8 here, and the two do different work: Deuteronomy gives 'choose', Jeremiah gives 'the way of ... and the way of ...'. Deuteronomy 30:19 as the source of Lehi's agency language was adjudicated at 2 Nephi 2:27; this row is placed on Jeremiah, which is where the wording of THIS verse is.
10:23.text: And unto this people thou shalt say, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death.

provenance.other: “reconciled to God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 5:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:20. Only 2 Corinthians has it as an imperative addressed to an audience — 'we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God' — which is the form 2 Nephi 10:24 takes.
provenance.significance: Paul's imperative is spoken by an ambassador standing in Christ's stead; Jacob's is spoken by a consecrated priest at the temple, at the end of a two-chapter sermon, and it is the sentence the whole sermon has been driving at. The reflexive is the departure: Paul says 'be ye reconciled', a passive, and Jacob says 'reconcile YOURSELVES', which puts the act on the hearer — and then immediately takes it back with 'it is only in and through the grace of God that ye are saved.'

10:24.note: The single most quoted line of the chapter, and its wording is 2 Corinthians 5:20's with the voice changed from passive to reflexive. That change is the argument of the verse, not an accident of paraphrase: the second half of the verse exists to qualify it.
10:24.text: Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.

provenance.other: “by grace are ye saved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 2:8 (the shorter 'by grace ye are saved' is Ephesians 2:5). The machine stream proposed Titus 2:11 for this verse on 'the grace of God that'; Titus has grace appearing, not grace saving, and is excluded.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 2:8-9 is the KJV's flat denial that salvation is 'of yourselves'. 2 Nephi 10:24 has just told its hearers to reconcile THEMSELVES to the will of God, and then answers the objection the imperative raises by quoting the one verse that forecloses it. The two halves of the verse are a reflexive command and its Pauline corrective, in that order.

10:24.note: 'It is only in and through the grace of God that ye are saved.' The adverbial 'only in and through' is not KJV, but 'the grace of God' and 'ye are saved' are Ephesians 2:8's, and the sentence performs the same argumentative move Ephesians 2:8-9 does. Split from the 2 Corinthians link because the two halves of the verse have different sources and the tension between them is the point.
10:24.text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:

provenance.other: “the power of his resurrection” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 3:10. 2 Nephi 10:25 has 'by the power of the resurrection', changing only the pronoun.
provenance.significance: Philippians 3:10-11 wants to know the power of his resurrection in order to 'attain unto the resurrection of the dead'. Jacob's closing benediction turns the phrase from an object of knowledge into an instrument of a blessing: 'may God raise you from death, by the power of the resurrection'.

10:25.note: One KJV verse in the whole Bible speaks of resurrection as a power; Jacob's benediction uses it as one. The parallel clause, 'and also from everlasting death, by the power of the atonement', builds a second phrase on the same pattern out of a word ('atonement') that the KJV never joins to 'power' — a good example of the book coining on a borrowed template.
10:25.text: That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death;

provenance.other: “everlasting kingdom” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Psalm 145:13, Daniel 4:3, Daniel 7:27, 2 Peter 1:11); only 2 Peter 1:11 is about a person being received into it. 'Divine' as an adjective is rare in the KJV — Proverbs 16:10, Hebrews 9:1, and 2 Peter 1:3 ('his divine power') and 1:4 ('the divine nature'); the other nineteen occurrences of the string are the verb, diviners and divination.
provenance.significance: The closing sentence takes three things from one short passage of 2 Peter: the entrance ministered into the everlasting kingdom (1:11), a power that is divine (1:3), and the adjective itself. 'Grace Divine', capitalized in the 1830 running text, is not a KJV phrase — but its adjective belongs, in this sense, almost solely to the passage the rest of the sentence comes from.

10:25.note: The Book of Mormon's 'received into the Eternal Kingdom of God' answers 2 Peter 1:11's 'an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom'; the substitution of 'eternal' for 'everlasting' is the departure. The n-gram stream proposed 2 Samuel 21:3 here on 'the atonement, that ye may' — the Gibeonite blood-price — which is excluded as wrong-sense.
10:25.text: For so an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
